No idea why I was asked to answer this one →_→, but here goes.


Here’s a story about a Nobel Prize.


The advisor: Robert Millikan, Nobel laureate and “inventor” of the oil-drop experiment;

The student: Harvey Fletcher, father of stereophonic sound, a former director at Bell Labs, and the real inventor of the oil-drop experiment.


In 1923, Millikan won the Nobel Prize in Physics for measuring the elementary charge with the oil-drop experiment. His student, Harvey Fletcher, was mentioned only as a collaborator. In fact, Fletcher was the one who really deserved the prize, because the oil-drop experiment came out of his PhD research. But Millikan struck a deal with him: Fletcher could put the oil-drop results in his thesis, but all the credit would go to the advisor. The secret came out only in the 1980s, when Fletcher died.


And another thing:

After Millikan’s 1923 Nobel Prize, scientists found that his result, the value of the elementary charge, was hard to reproduce. Only 60 years later did it come out that he had published the results of just 58 of his 140 experiments, because the rest deviated too much.


This story is so juicy and so outrageous that today it would hit the trending charts twice. I’ve already written the headlines:

— PhD’s deathbed confession blows the lid off academia’s darkest advisor–student secret

— Scientists worldwide sign petition over irreproducible results: can a dead Nobel laureate be recalled?


PS: He may have missed out on a Nobel and been bullied by his advisor, but Harvey Fletcher is a giant in acoustics: the father of stereophonic sound, a former director at Bell Labs, inventor of an audiometer and a hearing aid, and the man behind the equal-loudness contours (all you hi-fi fans, go and get acquainted). His contribution to psychoacoustics is immense.
